items.title: Unmasking EvilTokens: Getting to the root of device code phishing | Microsoft Security Blog
items.excerpt: This analysis dissects the EvilTokens infrastructure, revealing how threat actors exploit device code authentication flows to bypass multi-factor authentication and password-based defenses. The report details the technical mechanics of the phishing kit, infrastructure patterns, and detection strategies. IT defenders can use these insights to harden identity providers, deploy real-time alerting for suspicious device code requests, and block known malicious domains associated with the campaign.

items.title: Device Code Phishing is an Evolution in Identity Takeover | Proofpoint US
items.excerpt: Proofpoint examines how device code phishing has evolved into a primary vector for identity takeover, effectively neutralizing traditional MFA implementations. The article outlines attacker tactics, infrastructure reuse, and the shift toward cloud-native authentication exploitation. Defenders are advised to review OAuth consent grants, enforce phishing-resistant MFA, and implement user behavior analytics to detect anomalous authentication patterns across enterprise environments.

items.title: Microsoft 365 device code phishing campaign bypasses password stealing | RL Blog
items.excerpt: ReversingLabs details a targeted campaign leveraging Microsoft 365 device code flows to circumvent traditional credential harvesting techniques. By prompting users to authenticate directly on secondary devices, attackers bypass password stealers and capture valid session tokens. The report provides IOCs, infrastructure mappings, and mitigation guidance for securing enterprise identity platforms against this increasingly prevalent authentication bypass method.

items.title: GhostCode: Dissecting a Novel Device Code Phishing Kit | eSentire
items.excerpt: eSentire provides a technical breakdown of the GhostCode phishing kit, which automates device code generation and victim interaction. The analysis covers the kit’s architecture, evasion techniques, and deployment patterns. Infrastructure teams can leverage these findings to update web proxy filters, block associated C2 domains, and educate users on recognizing legitimate versus malicious device code prompts in corporate environments.

items.title: Sophisticated Spearphishing Campaign Targets Government Organizations, IGOs, and NGOs | CISA
items.excerpt: CISA warns of a highly targeted spearphishing campaign aimed at government bodies, international organizations, and NGOs. The campaign utilizes tailored lures and credential harvesting pages to compromise high-value accounts. Defenders should enforce strict email filtering, monitor for unusual login locations, and ensure privileged accounts utilize phishing-resistant authentication methods to prevent lateral movement and data exfiltration.

items.title: Russian state-supported cyber actors conduct phishing campaign targeting users of Zimbra collaboration suite
items.excerpt: The Australian Cyber Security Centre details a state-sponsored phishing campaign exploiting Zimbra collaboration suite users. Attackers deploy malicious links and credential harvesting pages to compromise email accounts. Infrastructure defenders should patch Zimbra instances, monitor for anomalous authentication attempts, and implement network segmentation to limit the impact of compromised collaboration platforms.

items.title: Email scammers posed as DOT officials in phishing messages focused on $1 trillion bill | CyberScoop
items.excerpt: CyberScoop reports on a phishing wave where attackers impersonated Department of Transportation officials, leveraging a major infrastructure funding bill as bait. The campaign targets financial and procurement personnel with malicious attachments and credential harvesting links. Organizations should verify sender authenticity, deploy advanced email security gateways, and conduct targeted awareness training to mitigate financial fraud and identity compromise risks.

items.title: CVE-2026-16720
items.excerpt: IBM API Connect 10.0.8.0 through 10.0.8.12 and 12.1.0.0 through 12.1.1.2 could allow a remote attacker to obtain valid access tokens for other users due to improper authentication. Authentication against a connected directory service is not sufficiently enforced, which could allow another user's identity to be assumed.

items.title: CVE-2026-8639
items.excerpt: IBM Security Verify Directory 10.0.0 through 10.0.4 and IBM Verify Directory 11.0.0 is vulnerable to session fixation. An attacker can establish a session and, after the victim authenticates, hijack the authenticated session to gain unauthorized access to the directory management console.

items.title: CVE-2026-123542
items.excerpt: OpenAM before 16.1.4 fails to enforce PKCE in the OAuth 2.0 device authorization flow, never validating the code verifier when device codes are exchanged for tokens. Attackers who obtain an approved device code from client logs or shared device storage can redeem it for access and ID tokens to impersonate the user.

items.title: CVE-2026-123538
items.excerpt: OpenAM before 16.1.4 does not verify that a signed SAML 1.x assertion or response was signed by the partner named as its issuer, accepting a signature from any certificate in OpenAM's keystore. An attacker holding such a private key, such as a trusted SAML 1.x partner, can forge assertions claiming another partner's issuer and sign in as that partner's users, including privileged ones.

items.title: CVE-2026-123553
items.excerpt: OpenAM before 16.1.4 ships built-in identities in the Top Level Realm (demo, anonymous, wsc, wsp, SecurityTokenService and agentAuth) with passwords that are identical on every installation, publicly known, and able to authenticate. Unauthenticated remote attackers can log in as these identities to obtain authenticated sessions, and the agent identities can read the configuration of other agent profiles.

items.title: CVE-2026-123544
items.excerpt: OpenAM before 16.1.4 and its client SDK fail to sufficiently validate responses on the internal server-to-server SOAP channel, allowing network-positioned attackers to affect integrity and availability. Attackers who intercept unencrypted traffic or control a site server can crash receiving processes, tamper with writable files, and possibly execute code.
